newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-FOCUS-Vote firms biggest Australian bank deal.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-FOCUS-Vote firms biggest Australian bank deal.

text.p: Advance Bank Ltd shareholders cleared the way for Australia's largest bank merger on Monday when they approved a scheme for St George Bank Ltd to make a cash and scrip offer worth A$2.65 billion.
Advance said polling showed nearly 90 percent of voting shareholders were in favour of the scheme which required a 75 percent margin to win approval.

The merger of the two Sydney-based regional banks would create Australia's fifth largest bank, with assets of A$40 billion and a market capitalisation of A$4.5 billion, making it one of Australia's top 25 listed companies.

Under the deal, Advance shareholders would be offered a combination of A$2.10 in cash, a 20 cent special cash dividend and new St George shares up to a value of A$5.00 per Advance share, giving a total value of about A$7.30.
The deal now requires the clearence of the Supreme Court of New South Wales on January 6 and two further procedural meetings for the Trustees of Advance's non-participating stock.
Last year, St George was foiled in its merger bid for Perth-based Challenge Bank Ltd when Westpac Banking Corp made a higher offer.
The latest merger plan includes a poison pill with Advance required to pay St George A$100 million if it were taken over by a third party.

Analysts said St George's eagerness to merge has been spurred by Australia's largest bank, National Australia Bank Ltd (NAB), which has been sniffing at St George's register since February and currently holds a 6.8 percent stake.
Asked if he was confident the deal would be successfully completed, a cautious St George chief, Jim Sweeney said, "I'm as confident as I can be. It's the first step in the dance."
Sweeney has reason to be cautious. St George has had five unsuccessful merger attempts in the past two years.

Most recently, St George's bid for Queensland-based regional, Metway Bank Ltd was scuttled by the Queensland government, which trumped its offer with a higher bid through its wholly-owned financial services group Suncorp and the Queensland Industry and Development Corp (QIDC).

NAB, which last week revealed a three-percent stake in Advance, has been seen as a possible blocker of the merger plan with analysts saying it was keen to put the deal on ice until the Wallis inquiry into Australia's finance and banking sector reported its findings in March.
Although St George's reaction to approval was cautious, the market was more confident with the consequences reflected in the share prices of the players involved.
"The approval appears to clinch the deal for St George and although this was bad for its shares, it was good for Advance and National Australia Bank stock," a Sydney based dealer said.
St George stock fell 19 cents to A$7.88 on Monday while Advance shares rose 16 cents to A$6.90 and NAB shares advanced 14 cents to A$14.63.

Possibly the most significant barrier to the proposed merger was removed before the start of the meeting by the Australian Securities Commission (ASC), when it said it would not oppose Advance's use of a deeming proxy provision.

Advance chairman, Jim Service told the meeting that the ASC had decided to appear at the court hearing on January 6, but would not oppose the use of the mechanism, which allows Advance to vote proxies obtained from Monday's meeting at the later meetings to alter its articles of association.
Advance decided to adopt the deemed proxy procedure to stop the possibility of a single shareholder frustrating the deal at the later meetings.
